Pele Yoetz 198:15: [3] Four conditions must be present in every single commandment in order to perform it properly, so that it be accepted with favor before our Father, our King, our Maker, may His Name be blessed, and one not be locked out with shame in the World to Come:
Pele Yoetz 198:16: 1. That every commandment be done with the intention of fulfilling the duty of what our Maker commanded us to do, to give delight to our Maker and to repair matters as ordained in the supernal realm.
Pele Yoetz 198:17: 2. Let him see how even a tiny gnat, diminished from mere breath, a vessel full of shame, stands to serve before the exalted and uplifted King, while the angels on high answer in dread, etc., with a great commotion.
Pele Yoetz 198:18: 3. Love for the perfect King who abounds in doing good, who chooses His people Israel with love, and in His love and compassion has bestowed upon us goodness without measure. And above all, that He chose us from among all the nations and sanctified us with His commandments. And they said in the holy Zohar that any commandment not performed with awe and love is not a [true] commandment and does not fly upward; and especially with Torah and prayer, if the voice is heard without awe and love, of it is written (Numbers 11:1), “And the Lord heard, and His wrath burned,” God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 198:19: 4. One must rejoice with great joy in performing a commandment, for every commandment that comes his way is a gift sent to him by the Holy One, blessed be He, and according to the abundance of joy, so his reward will be great. And Rabbi Isaac Luria, of blessed memory, revealed that everything he attained — that the gates of wisdom and the holy spirit were opened to him — came about because he rejoiced in performing every commandment with boundless joy. Thus it is fitting to rejoice more than over all gold and abundant fine gold, by reflecting deeply on for whose sake the King of the world went forth, desiring closeness to Him, to stand and serve Him and to love Him. Happy is one born of woman whom the great, mighty and awesome King has given dominion over the works of His hands, putting everything under his feet (Psalms 8:7), that he may build his chambers in heaven and give delight to his Maker for his own benefit and good — truly there is no good and no joy greater than this. And the Tanna spoke well (Avot 4:17): “Better one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come.”
Pele Yoetz 198:20: [4] Positive commandments from the Torah that depend on the heart and can be fulfilled every day (besides those already mentioned): Part of the fear of Heaven is not to utter the Name of Heaven except with fear of heart, for great need and not in vain. And the prohibition against invoking the Lord's Name in vain applies in any language, whether in a needless oath, a false oath, a curse, or idle words, or one who recites an unnecessary blessing, or a truncated and clipped blessing that is invalid. Likewise, part of the fear of Heaven is that one should fear and dread transgressing His will to His face. Let a man tremble and take hold of himself, and let trembling seize him: how could even a small gnat, diminished as a mere breath, anger the exalted and uplifted King? Part of love is that, out of great longing for love of Him, blessed be He, one drives sleep from his eyes in order to engage in His Torah and delight in it.
Pele Yoetz 198:21: Likewise, part of love is that one give all the wealth of his house out of love, and his body, spirit and soul — all should be considered as nothing to him compared to doing his Maker's will, and he should say, “When will it come to my hand to perform a commandment for the favor and delight of my beloved, the Rock of my heart? My soul longs for You day and night, to cling to You and to find Your will.” Part of the commandment of “and you shall love” is that he should cause others to love the blessed Name, by teaching them Torah and words that subdue [the evil inclination].
Pele Yoetz 198:22: It is a commandment to cling to the blessed Name, that one should remember the blessed Name always, never separating from Him. It is a commandment to cling to Torah scholars in order to learn from their deeds. And included in this is that one should marry the daughter of a Torah scholar, marry off his daughter to a Torah scholar, do business on behalf of a Torah scholar, and associate and cling to them, for clinging to them is as though clinging to the Divine Presence (Sifrei and Rashi, Eikev 11:22). It is a commandment to fear a Torah scholar. It is a commandment to love the Torah scholar.
Pele Yoetz 198:23: It is a commandment to focus on the first verse of the recitation of Shema and to lengthen the word “echad” (One) in order to crown the Lord above and below and in the four directions, and to consider that he is ready with a whole heart to give his life for the sanctification of the Name. It is a commandment to have intention in prayer, since the Holy One, blessed be He, made it dependent on the heart, as it is written (Deuteronomy 11:13), “And to serve Him with all your heart.” It is a commandment to resemble Him, blessed be He, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:9), “And you shall walk in His ways.” Our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Shabbat 133b): just as He is merciful, so you be merciful; just as He is pious, so you be pious. It is a commandment to be in the synagogue with awe and gravity, out of dread of the blessed Name who dwells within it. It is a commandment to trust in the blessed Name with a whole heart in all the affairs of the world.
Pele Yoetz 198:24: It is a commandment to remember and reflect upon His greatness, blessed be He. It is a commandment to remember the kindnesses of the Lord that He has done and does for all Israel and for each individual from the time he was formed in his mother's womb. It is a commandment to remember, with a trembling heart, the exodus from Egypt every day and every night. It is a commandment to fear one's father and mother, and to tremble and be greatly afraid of transgressing their will. The commandment “and you shall love your fellow as yourself” with a whole heart, and from this: “what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow” (Shabbat 31a). It is a commandment to judge every person favorably (Avot 1:6). It is a commandment to justify the [divine] judgment for whatever happens, whether to his body, his children, or his money, and not to attribute it to chance, but rather to examine his deeds and repent. “And you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16) — that a person's heart should be soft to accept the words of the one who rebukes him and not hate him; on the contrary, he should increase his love for him, in the manner of “rebuke a wise man and he will love you” (Proverbs 9:8). It is a commandment to remember the day of Shabbat in one's heart at all times. It is a commandment that the sinner turn from his sin and feel great remorse and firmly resolve never to sin again until his dying day. And every single day a heavenly voice proclaims, “Return, wayward children.” Therefore let every man tremble and repent and bring others back from sin as much as is in his power, with sweetness of speech, and find favor in the eyes of the King of the world, and happy is his portion.
Pele Yoetz 198:25: The commandment of honoring father and mother — its essence is that they be honored in his eyes, that he love them with an intense love, and that they not be a burden and a load upon him. It is a commandment to feel pain over a fellow's pain, a genuine pain of soul, especially if he is a Torah scholar, so that he pray for mercy on his behalf and support and help him as he is able. It is a commandment that a person be always calm and composed, removing anger from his heart, so that even his flesh may dwell securely. It is a commandment to accept upon oneself the yoke of the commandments by reciting the passage “And it shall come to pass, if you hearken,” as it is said (Deuteronomy 11:18), “And you shall place these My words upon your heart.” It is a commandment that a person consider every day that he is a servant sealed to the King of the world with the seal of the desire of the holy covenant, and not rebel against Him. It is a commandment to bring to mind every day the matter of Miriam and her punishment, so that his mouth be shut and he tremble at speaking slander, for it is a great sin, and of it is said (Job 19:29), “Be afraid of the sword for yourselves.” And whoever is understanding will hold onto this and receive good reward in this world and the World to Come, his understanding being good.
Pele Yoetz 198:26: [5] Negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the heart and can be kept every day: That it should not enter one's mind that there is a god besides the Lord. Not to covet what belongs to our brethren the children of Israel, and not to plan or strive to take it from him whether for payment or for free. Not to forget the Lord even for a moment, in order to acquire for one's soul the conduct required by remembrance, such as fear, modesty, honest thoughts and correction of one's traits, as befits one who stands before Him. Not to forget the awesome standing at Mount Sinai, where our God gave us the Torah there. Not to forget any part of its study, by being idle from Torah and not meditating on it always. Not to remove from our hearts the evil that Amalek did to us, and when we have the strength, we shall avenge ourselves upon him. Not to forget that we provoked the Lord to wrath in the wilderness, and how much more should we remember our own deeds and be ashamed. Not to forget the leprosy of Miriam, so that we be careful about slander. Not to be haughty, for this is like worshipping idolatry, and one is under a ban according to the sages of the Talmud (Sotah 4b, 5a). Not to become angry, for all calm comes from the side of holiness, and all wrath from the side of impurity; and the heart is a sanctuary for the Divine Presence, so one who becomes angry brings an idol into the sanctuary and drives the Divine Presence from it. Therefore let every man tremble and not become angry, neither with a gentile nor with an Israelite, neither with the small nor the great, not over robbery or fraud, and not over withheld honor, or even if they curse and revile him; rather let his mind be calm and settled, and thereby the Lord his God is with him and the shout of a King is among him. Not to test the Lord by saying, “I will do good deeds and see if good comes to me from the Lord” — except regarding tithes, where it is written (Malachi 3:10), “Test Me now in this.”
Pele Yoetz 198:27: Not to hate a fellow Israelite. And we have been warned to remove hatred from our hearts, for it engenders many sins; therefore our Maker commanded us not to take revenge and not to bear a grudge, not to accept slander and not to believe evil of one's fellow, but only to be wary and take precaution. That we should not have the trait of cruelty, but rather have mercy on one who is in distress. That we should not have a stingy eye when it comes to lending to the poor and giving charity and doing kindness and the like, but rather spend on a commandment with a generous eye. Not to entertain evil thoughts, and if they come to him, he should push them away at once with both hands, for they defile the soul and cause impurity at night. That a person should not despair of mercy even if he sees trouble approaching, but rather hope for the Lord's salvation. That we should not be afraid to render righteous judgment, for we believe that no harm will befall us in performing commandments, since agents on a mission of a commandment are not harmed. That the idolaters should never find favor if they have ever tried to entice, as is the custom of the nations who tell Israel to convert. Not to have pity or mercy on those who cause others to sin or lead them astray. Not to spare one who deserves to be punished and disciplined. Not to be righteous in one's own eyes. Not to hate rebuke or the one who rebukes, for “the reproofs of instruction are the way of life” (Proverbs 6:23); through them there is a straight path — “it is a tree of life to those who grasp it, and those who hold fast to it are happy.”
Pele Yoetz 198:28: [6] Positive commandments from the words of Kabbalah and from the words of the Sages that depend on the heart and can be fulfilled every day: A person should always incite his good inclination against his evil inclination (Berachot 5a). A person should always be shrewd in his fear of Heaven (ibid. 17a). It is stated in the holy Zohar that when a person is enjoying himself at his table, he should remember and grieve over the holy land and the King's palace that lies destroyed. And because of that sadness he feels at his table, the Holy One, blessed be He, considers it as though he had rebuilt His house — happy is his portion. One should not stand up to pray except out of gravity of mind (Berachot 30a), meaning humility. And “rejoice with trembling” — where there is joy, there should be trembling too, such as at a wedding feast or a circumcision, lest one sin from the joy of his heart. “Serve the Lord with joy” — the joy of a commandment, that he be glad and rejoice that he has merited to be a servant to a King like whom there is none in the world, while on the other hand he should be humble and fear and dread over how he angered Him at first. It is a commandment that a person be despised and loathsome in his own eyes, and honor those who fear the Lord (Psalms 15:4) — that whoever is known to be God-fearing should be considered important and highly honored in his eyes. And he should be humble before every person, so that every person seem greater to him than himself, and he should feel shame before him and fear him. Every matter, whether of commandment or of optional activity, should be weighed before it leaves his mouth, whether it is proper to say and how it should be said. All your deeds, even mundane ones, should be for the sake of Heaven. “In all your ways know Him” (Proverbs 3:6). It is a commandment to rejoice in suffering, as it is said (Psalms 101:1), “I will sing of kindness and justice.” Let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own (Avot 2:12), and your fellow's honor like the reverence due your teacher, and the reverence due your teacher like the reverence due Heaven (ibid. 4:12). Be bold as a leopard and mighty as a lion to do the will of your Father in Heaven, but regarding mundane matters, boldness of face leads to Gehinnom and shamefacedness to the Garden of Eden (ibid. 5:20). Reflect on three things: know what is above you — a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and all your deeds are written in a book (ibid. 3:1). Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to Torah (ibid. 1:12). Receive every person with a pleasant countenance (ibid., v. 15). Weigh the loss of a commandment against its reward, and the reward of a transgression against its loss (ibid. 2:1) — this is a great principle of the Torah. A person should love his neighbors and draw his relatives close. If his fellow did him a small kindness, let it seem great in his eyes. A person's heart should be broad and slow to anger, and he should be among those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their disgrace and do not respond (Shabbat 88b), and he should rejoice in suffering and accept it with love, and believe with a whole heart and say, “This too is for the good,” for whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good (Berachot 60b). It is a commandment to be envious of those who fear the Lord, in order to be like them. A person should love his wife as his own body, and honor her and clothe her more than his own body. It is a good path for a person to cling to a good heart, and within it the entire Torah is contained, for he will take to heart what his duty is and perform it as is proper. The blessed Name commanded through His prophets that a person hope for and anticipate the salvation of Israel through the coming of our Messiah every day, as it is said (Habakkuk 2:3), “Though he tarry, wait for him, for he shall surely come” — so may it be [His] will, speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 198:29: [7] Negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and from the words of the Sages that depend on the heart, and can be fulfilled every day: “Rejoice not, O Israel, to exultation like the nations” (Hosea 9:1) — we are not permitted to rejoice except with the joy of a commandment. Do not take to heart all the words people say, even one who curses you, even if he is your own servant, for if you take their words to heart, you will become angry and thereby withhold the light of the soul's wisdom. Do not despair of retribution (Avot 1:7), for a person should always consider that he is subject to whatever evils are stirring to come upon the world. Happy is the man who is always fearful. Do not scorn any person, small or great, gentile or Israelite, for there is no man who does not have his hour (ibid. 4:3). Do not be wise in your own eyes (Proverbs 3:7), for “there is more hope for a fool than for a man wise in his own eyes” (ibid. 26:12), and “listen to the counsel of the wise” (ibid. 12:15). Do not trust in yourself until the day you die (Avot 2:4). Do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place (ibid.). Do not make your prayer a fixed routine and a burden upon you, wondering when you will cast it off, but rather [make it] a supplication before the Lord (ibid. 2:13). “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice” (Proverbs 24:17), and “he who rejoices at calamity will not go unpunished” (ibid. 17:5). Do not be like a horse or a mule without understanding at the time of intimacy, but rather intend it for the sake of the commandment, with modesty and holiness. Envy, lust and honor drive a person out of this world and out of the World to Come. If you have studied much Torah and increased in commandments and good deeds, do not take credit for yourself, for it is for this purpose that you were created (Avot 2:8). Do not be like servants who serve their master on condition of receiving a reward (ibid. 1:3). Do not worry about tomorrow's trouble, for you do not know what a day may bring forth (Yevamot 63b). “My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord, and do not loathe His rebuke; for the one whom the Lord loves He rebukes, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:11-12).
Pele Yoetz 198:30: [8] Positive commandments from the Torah that depend on the eyes and can be fulfilled every day: To look at the tzitzit in order to remember the commandments, as it is written (Numbers 15:39), “And you shall see it and remember” — seeing leads to remembering (Menachot 43b). It is a commandment to read the Written Torah from the written text itself. It is a commandment to weep over a worthy person and over the suffering of the righteous, as though they were one's own children.
Pele Yoetz 198:31: [9] Negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the eyes: Not to stray after the sight of one's eyes, and not to gaze at forbidden relations — not only for the sake of lust, but even not for the sake of lust, merely deriving pleasure from the gazing. Not to gaze upon images of idol worship. Not to gaze upon the garments of a woman one knows.
Pele Yoetz 198:32: [10] Positive and negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the eyes: One must be careful that his eyes be closed during prayer out of dread of the Divine Presence, or that he keep his eyes specifically within the prayer book. Before beginning the Amidah, he should reflect and humble his heart. Part of the ways of humility is to lower one's eyes and not look beyond four cubits, and this is very helpful in acquiring an order of holiness. At the time of responding to Kedushah, he should close his eyes and lift them heavenward with intention and longing to cling to the blessed Name. Not to gaze at an animal, beast or fowl when they are mating. Not to gaze at the moon, except when saying “when I see Your heavens.” It is forbidden to gaze at the hands of the kohanim during the Priestly Blessing, even nowadays. It is forbidden to gaze at the face of a wicked person, and certainly at the face of an idolater. One should not gaze at a person while he is eating or at his portion, so as not to embarrass him. And do not seek to see him at the time of his disgrace, and the same applies to anything where there is concern that a person feels shame or pain; rather let the spirit of humankind be at ease with him, and thereby the spirit of the Omnipresent will be at ease with him.
Pele Yoetz 198:33: [11] Positive and negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the ears: It is a commandment to hear words of Torah in order to keep and fulfill them. Also, that one's ear should hear the rebuke of instruction (see Proverbs 15:31). It is a commandment that if a person hears something improper, he should put his finger in his ears; and we have been warned not to listen to any slander or disparaging words about one's fellow. It is a commandment to heed the judgments that arise for Israel in every generation. The commandments of Grace after Meals, the blessing over the Torah, and the recitation of Shema also depend on the ear, for one must make his ears hear it. Not to listen to one who incites [to idolatry]. A warning to a judge not to hear the words of one litigant before the other litigant arrives (Sanhedrin 7b).
Pele Yoetz 198:34: [12] Positive and negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the ears: It is a commandment to incline one's ear and listen to the reading of the Torah scroll from the mouth of the prayer leader as though receiving it now from the mouth of the Lord at Sinai, and to be silent as one who has no mouth. To incline one's ear to the prayer leader's recitation and to all blessings, for if one does not sense and know to which blessing he is responding, his “Amen” is an orphaned one. It is a commandment regarding all blessings that one make his own ears hear them and make others hear them so that they may answer “Amen.” “Hear counsel and accept discipline, that you may be wise in the end” (Proverbs 19:20). A person should not let idle words reach his ears, for they are the first to be burned among his limbs (Ketubot 5b). One who hears vulgar speech and remains silent falls into Gehinnom. A woman's voice is a form of nakedness, and it is forbidden to listen to it. Since the destruction of the Temple, our sages forbade listening to musical instruments and every kind of sound-producing device — it is forbidden to use them for rejoicing and forbidden to listen to them, and even singing with the mouth is forbidden unless it is a song and praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the ear that listens to a mundane song of this kind should be uprooted. Then “our mouths shall be filled with laughter and our tongues with joyous song” (Psalms 126:2), when the Temple is rebuilt speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 198:35: [13] Positive commandments from the Torah that depend on the mouth and throat and can be fulfilled every day: The commandment of honoring father and mother, and one's father's wife, and one's mother's husband, and one's father's brother and sister, and one's mother's brother and sister, and one's grandfather and grandmother on both sides, and one's father-in-law and mother-in-law, one's older brother, and anyone greater than him in wisdom or in age — that he honor them in speech, speaking to them gently, with soft, respectful and dignified language, as one would address a king. It is a commandment to mention the exodus from Egypt by day and by night. It is a commandment to recite Grace after Meals calmly, aloud, and with joy of heart. It is a commandment to recite the blessing over the Torah. It is a commandment to study Torah. It is a commandment to teach others. The commandment of Torah study outweighs all other commandments, and the sin of neglecting Torah study outweighs all other transgressions. It is a commandment to recite the Shema morning and evening. It is a commandment for the kohanim to bless Israel (Yerushalmi Megillah, end of ch. 4). It is a commandment for one qualified to render halachic rulings to serve as a halachic authority. It is a commandment to recall aloud every day what Amalek did to us, may his name be blotted out. It is a commandment to remember how our ancestors provoked the blessed Name to anger in the wilderness, and how much more so how we and our ancestors provoked Him. It is a commandment to remember what the Lord did to Miriam, so that we be careful about slander. It is a commandment to confess and to specify one's sin.
Pele Yoetz 198:36: The commandment of rebuke: one is obligated to rebuke a fellow who wronged him or his relative, or who spoke ill of him to his face or behind his back, in the manner of “and Abraham rebuked Abimelech” (Genesis 21:25); perhaps he will accept the rebuke and say, “I have sinned against you,” or excuse himself — he should not bear him a grudge, nor stay silent and conceal his hatred in his heart, for that is the way of the wicked. The commandment of rebuke also applies to one who sees his fellow sinning or going in a bad way — he must bring him back to good privately, between the two of them, gently and with soft language. It is a commandment, when there is a dispute among the sages of Israel, to follow one's own rabbi. It is a commandment for one who has knowledge of testimony on behalf of his fellow to testify in court in a way that the judgment can be established upon his testimony. It is a commandment to examine and question the witnesses thoroughly when it appears that the judgment involves deceit, in order to bring the truth of the matter to light. It is a commandment to adjudicate all monetary matters between man and his fellow. It is a commandment to sanctify the kohanim and treat them with honor. And speak comfortingly to the sick, if such speech is beneficial to them. It is a commandment to bring the sick person to repentance. It is a commandment to eulogize a worthy person who has died.
Pele Yoetz 198:37: The commandment of prayer, that one weigh every single word as though counting gold coins. It is a commandment to mention the blessed Name aloud, reciting from time to time, in order to arouse love, verses recalling our Maker and His fear, blessed be He, such as “the whole earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3), “great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open upon all the ways of men, to give to every man according to his ways” (Jeremiah 32:19), “happy is the man who does not forget You, and the son of man who strengthens himself in You,” “happy is the man who heeds Your commandment, and takes Your Torah and Your word to heart,” and the like. It is a commandment to appoint judges and also officers to enforce judicial rulings. It is a commandment to seek peace and pursue peace and to make peace between a man and his wife and between one person and another. And whoever wishes to merit the ways of peace should be careful always to judge every person favorably. It is a commandment to make a vow at a time of distress, though it is better not to vow at all. It is a commandment that one's mouth and heart be in accord, and that he not speak one thing with his mouth while thinking another in his heart. It is a commandment to remember Shabbat every day in every way one can mention it, such as not naming the days of the week in the language of the gentiles, but rather saying “First day toward holy Shabbat,” “Second day toward holy Shabbat,” and so on. Likewise, when something good comes a person's way, he should set it aside and say aloud, “This is for Shabbat.” Regarding a debt over which the Sabbatical year has passed and his fellow comes to repay it, it is a commandment to say, “I release you [from the debt], I do not want it.” And if his fellow says, “Nevertheless,” he should accept it. Likewise, a murderer (and the same applies to other transgressors) who moved from his place to another place and people wished to honor him, should say to them, “I am a murderer, I am not worthy of honor.” And if they say, “Nevertheless,” he should accept it. It is a positive commandment to cry out and sound an alarm before the Lord in assembly over any trouble that comes upon the community, so that the entire people take to heart that this is not mere chance, but rather the decree of the King of the world on account of sins, and that they turn from their evil ways and walk in the way of the good.
Pele Yoetz 198:38: [14] Negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the mouth and throat and can be kept every day:
Pele Yoetz 198:39: Not to swear in vain or falsely. And it is forbidden for one who knows he cannot truthfully take an oath in court, when the oath is imposed on him, to say “I will swear” in order to frighten his fellow, even though he has no intention of actually swearing, for this too is included in “you shall not take [in vain],” which means “you shall not accept.” One who recites an unnecessary blessing transgresses “you shall not take [in vain],” and likewise one who invokes the Name of Heaven in vain, and likewise one who causes his fellow to swear needlessly. One who swears and does not fulfill his oath transgresses the prohibition of a false oath. Not to curse any person, even when not in his presence, and certainly to his face; and there is an additional prohibition for one who curses himself, and an additional prohibition for one who curses a judge or the head of an academy, and an additional prohibition for one who curses his father or mother; and this applies not only to one who curses them, but even to one who belittles their honor and does not honor them properly — of him it is said (Deuteronomy 27:16), “Cursed be he who dishonors his father or mother.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shevuot 36a) that “cursed” implies excommunication. Therefore let every man tremble lest he be excommunicated in Heaven if he shows disrespect toward them. “You shall not afflict any widow or orphan” (Exodus 22:21) — and speaking to them harshly is a form of affliction. “You shall not wrong one another” (Leviticus 25:17) — our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Bava Metzia 58b) that this means not to cause him pain with words (unless it is to rebuke him and guide him in a good way). Not to embarrass one's fellow publicly even when rebuking him to bring him back from sin. One who gives his fellow a demeaning name or embarrasses him has no share in the World to Come (ibid.). “You shall not testify in a dispute” (Exodus 23:2) — rather one should be among those who hear their disgrace and do not respond, so that the quarrel not intensify. Not to testify alone, for since he is not deemed reliable [alone], he is considered as one who spreads a bad name, unless it is meant to prevent a transgression or concerns a monetary matter. Not to give one's fellow improper advice. Not to speak slander.
Pele Yoetz 198:40: That one should present his case to the court only when his fellow [litigant] is present with him (Sanhedrin 7b). Not to argue one party's case for him. Not to spread a bad name. That judgment should not be lenient toward one party and harsh toward the other (Sanhedrin, ibid.). Not to mention the name of an idol unless one renames it with a demeaning term. It is forbidden to form a partnership with a gentile, lest an oath become due from him and he swear by the name of an idol, thereby transgressing “let it not be heard from your mouth” (Exodus 23:13). One who persists in a dispute transgresses “and let him not be like Korah” (Numbers 17:5). Not to lie. Not to deny holding money belonging to another. Not to swear a false denial of a monetary debt (these transgressions follow from theft; one who steals will eventually deny it and swear falsely). Not to strengthen the hands of transgressors nor associate with those who condone injustice. Not to flatter, for one who flatters brings wrath upon the world. And if he cannot protest, let him at least remain silent, and not call evil good. Not to speak vulgar speech, for it brings suffering and destruction upon the world, and Heaven above places a ban upon him, God forbid. Not to practice divination and not to rely on omens and vanities, either to refrain from an action or to perform one. Not to practice astrology, saying “this hour is good to begin this deed” and “this one is not good,” but rather to trust in the blessed Name in all his affairs. Not to show people something that is not so, by way of trickery and frivolity. Not to whisper over a wound while reciting a verse from the Torah. Not to appoint as a judge someone who is not expert in the laws. Not to render a ruling that is against the law, and our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot, beginning of ch. 1), “Be deliberate in judgment.” A judge should not rule while intoxicated, whenever he senses that he is somewhat intoxicated, and one who judges after eating and drinking [to excess] is as though he destroys the world. Judgment should not be perverted, especially regarding a convert or an orphan. Not to accept the testimony of a wicked person and not to testify together with a wicked person. And anyone who has committed a transgression punishable by lashes, or a thief, robber, or one who lends with interest, is termed wicked and disqualified from testifying. A relative should not testify. Not to utter holy words while naked, or facing nakedness, or facing excrement or urine. Not to press a poor person whom one knows is unable to repay, and it is even forbidden to pass before him, lest he think one has come to demand payment and become frightened. A person should not be an intermediary between borrower and lender in an interest transaction, nor a witness, scribe, or guarantor for it. One should not remain silent when he could say something that would prevent his fellow from losing money in any way, and certainly to prevent harm to his body, and all the more so to his life, as it is said (Leviticus 19:16), “You shall not stand idly by your fellow's blood.” Not to demand a loan whose Sabbatical-year term has passed. Not to draft a groom from his home for optional duties during the first year, and the groom himself is also warned not to leave, as it is said (Deuteronomy 24:5), “he shall be free for his house.”
Pele Yoetz 198:41: [15] Positive commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the mouth and throat, which can be fulfilled every day:
Pele Yoetz 198:42: One who mentions a righteous person should bless him, and one who mentions a wicked person must curse him, as it is said (Proverbs 10:6), “The memory of the righteous is for a blessing, but the name of the wicked shall rot.” It is a commandment to comfort a poor person with words. It is a commandment to greet every person first, even a gentile in the marketplace. It is a commandment to answer gently one who speaks harshly, and to increase peace with one's brothers, relatives, and everyone. It is a commandment for a person to acquire a friend for himself, to read with him and eat with him and reveal his secrets to him, and the essential means of acquiring this is through sweetness of speech. It is a commandment to change [the facts] for the sake of peace (Yevamot 65b). It is a commandment to recite blessings over pleasures beforehand in any amount, and afterward when the amount reaches an olive's or a quarter-log's volume. It is a commandment to recite all the blessings of praise and the blessings over commandments that our sages, of blessed memory, instituted for us, letter by letter, word by word. It is a commandment to invite [zimun for Grace after Meals]. It is a commandment to answer “Amen” and “Blessed is He and blessed is His Name.” It is a commandment for one with a pleasant voice to sing before the Lord. It is a commandment to lament the destruction of the Temple and the exile of the Divine Presence. It is a commandment to fall asleep amid words of Torah and the recitation of Shema, and not to interrupt with mundane speech. It is a commandment to rise to engage in Torah at the first watch of the night and to supplicate then for the Sanctuary and for Israel. “A fool answers according to his folly” in words of Torah lest he remain in his error and mislead others, but regarding mundane matters, do not answer him [according to his folly]. It is a commandment to speak words of Torah at the table. “Say to wisdom, you are my sister” (Proverbs 7:4) — if a matter is as clear to you as your sister, who is forbidden to you, say it; if not, remain silent (Kiddushin 30b). It is a commandment to make the effort to explain the reasons of matters to one's students. It is a commandment to review one's studies aloud, so that it is arranged throughout his 248 limbs, and to recite with melody and song. It is a commandment for a person to conduct himself, speaking calmly and composedly to every person, as one speaking before the King, who would be afraid to raise his voice before Him, for the whole earth is full of His glory. It is a commandment for a person to ask for his sustenance from the blessed Name morning and evening, and for this our sages instituted the psalm “A Psalm of Praise, of David” (Psalms 145:1), which must be recited with the intention of a poor man asking. One who goes on a journey, it is a commandment for him to recite the Traveler's Prayer. Four types of people must give thanks (Berachot 54b), and it is good to thank the Lord for granting us relief, salvation, and all good things. It is a commandment to answer “Amen, yehei shmei rabba” with all one's strength. It is a commandment to recite Kiddush and Havdalah over wine on Shabbat and festivals. Moses instituted for Israel that they read the laws of each festival in its proper time (Megillah 32a) — how good is a word fitly spoken.
Pele Yoetz 198:43: [16] Negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the mouth and throat: Not to say something without attributing it to the one who said it. Just as it is a commandment to say something that will be heeded, so it is a commandment not to say something that will not be heeded (Yevamot 65b; Yerushalmi Chagigah, end of ch. 1), for it is better that people err unintentionally. Do not rush into a dispute; patience, patience — it is worth four hundred zuz (Berachot 20a). Do not make yourself like those who argue cases before judges (Avot 1:8). Do not let your mouth bring your flesh into guilt through vows. One who interrupts his Torah study for idle matters endangers his own life (ibid. 3:6). One does not converse in the privy. It is forbidden to interrupt between [the blessing of] redemption and prayer, and between the tefillin of the arm and the tefillin of the head, even to answer Kaddish or Kedushah. It is forbidden to speak in the middle of Pesukei D'Zimrah, during the repetition of the Amidah, and while the reader is reading from the Torah scroll, and certainly during the recitation of Shema and its blessings, the Amidah prayer, Hallel, the falling on one's face [Tachanun], Grace after Meals, and the like. It is forbidden to raise or make one's voice heard during prayer. It is forbidden to speak mundane matters, and certainly to raise one's voice, in the synagogue. Do not scorn any person (Avot 4:3), neither great nor small, neither Israelite nor gentile; rather, regard every person in your eyes as a robber to be guarded against, and receive every person with a pleasant countenance and honor them as Rabban Gamliel did (ibid. 1:15). Do not converse excessively with a woman (Nedarim 20a; Avot 1:5). Regarding even one's own ritually pure wife they said this, how much more so a niddah, and how much more so another man's wife — even for a necessary purpose one should speak with any woman only briefly. It is forbidden to speak idle words. A person should not open his mouth to Satan [by speaking of potential misfortune] (Berachot 19a). Do not quarrel with a person for no reason if he has not done you harm. They said (Nedarim 22a) that there is no harm except Gehinnom, meaning if he caused you to sin; but for a needless matter, if he damaged your body or your money, do not quarrel with me [over it], for it is all vanity — only one who causes another to sin is worse than one who kills him. It is forbidden to teach a case against Israel, even a generation of the wicked, God forbid. Do not say to your fellow, “Go and come back, and tomorrow I will give,” [when you have it now]. Not to conduct business talk on Shabbat, and even idle chatter is forbidden, for it was only under pressing circumstances that they permitted greetings on Shabbat, and the Zohar calls idle words a desecration of Shabbat. It is forbidden to be lazy in eulogizing a worthy person. It is forbidden to count Israelites even for the purpose of a commandment. It is forbidden to greet a wicked enemy, though for the sake of peace it is proper to give the greeting when it is one's own teacher [who is greeted first], or [one may reinterpret it as directed] to the blessed Name, as it is said (I Samuel 25:6), “And you shall say thus: to life!” [“Lechai”] — David told them to intend it for the Life of the worlds, and [say to the person] “peace to you.” It is forbidden to deceive people's minds, even the mind of a gentile; rather, be wholehearted, and the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 198:44: [17] Positive commandments from the Torah that depend on the gullet: It is a commandment to give food to an animal, beast or fowl whose feeding is one's responsibility, before he himself tastes anything, and certainly it is forbidden to cause any living creature pain with one's own hands, for the prohibition against causing pain to animals is from the Torah. It is a commandment to eat and drink on Shabbat and festivals, and one must eat three meals on Shabbat. One who omits one of the three meals is greatly punished, and whoever delights in Shabbat is greatly rewarded (Shabbat 118a). It is a commandment to eat and drink on Rosh Chodesh. It is a commandment to eat and drink on the eve of Yom Kippur. It is a commandment to eat an olive's volume of matzah on the first night of Passover. It is a commandment to eat an olive's volume of bread in the sukkah on the first night of Sukkot. It is the commandment of affliction from eating and drinking on Yom Kippur. To abstain from eating chametz on Passover. It is a commandment to refrain from eating an impure animal, an impure fowl, and an impure fish. It is a commandment, when eating meat, to eat the meat of an animal ritually slaughtered.
Pele Yoetz 198:45: [18] Negative commandments that depend on the mouth and gullet: At the time a person refrains from forbidden things, he should intend in his heart that he refrains because of the blessed Name's command, in order to do His will and give delight before His Throne of Glory: Not to eat forbidden fat. Not to eat blood. Not to eat any carcass, and included in this is not to eat an animal born until seven days have passed. Not to eat a torn or mortally wounded animal. Not to eat the sciatic sinew. Not to eat a limb from a living animal. Not to eat meat with milk. Not to eat an impure animal, impure fowl, impure fish, and every kind of detestable creeping thing. Not to eat orlah fruit for three years. Not to eat from the new grain crop until the sixteenth of Nisan has passed. Not to eat food offered to idols and not to drink wine used for idolatrous libation. Not to eat anything involving a risk to life, for danger to life is treated more stringently than a [ritual] prohibition (Chullin 10a), as it is written (Deuteronomy 4:15), “And you shall greatly guard your souls.” Not to eat an unblemished firstborn animal, or one in which a blemish was deliberately inflicted. Not to derive benefit from the dead, his grave, or his shrouds. Not to be a glutton and a drunkard. Not to eat from an animal before its life has departed. Not to eat or drink disgusting things, or from a disgusting vessel. Not to eat chametz on the eve of Passover from midday until the end of the 21st of Nisan. Not to eat or drink on Yom Kippur. Not to eat from when dawn breaks until one has prayed the morning prayer.
Pele Yoetz 198:46: [19] Positive and negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the mouth and gullet: To delight in Shabbat with good foods, pleasant to the palate. The commandment of the fourth meal at the conclusion of Shabbat, that one should set a table even for a mere olive's volume. The commandment of the Purim feast. To eat the wedding feast and the circumcision feast. The four cups on the night of Passover. Eating maror. Dipping in charoset. To drink the wine of Kiddush, the wine of Havdalah, and the cup of Grace after Meals. To fast over every trouble that comes upon the community on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, until mercy comes from Heaven, and not to treat it as mere chance, saying “it is happenstance.” To observe the four fasts and to return to the Lord through fasting for as many days as one can bear, in order to restrain transgression and put an end to sin. The Sages said (Chullin 93a) that certain threads and membranes are forbidden due to the prohibition of forbidden fat, and others due to the prohibition of blood and the fat of the sciatic sinew. And meat that has sat for three days without being soaked in water in between may only be eaten roasted. It is forbidden to eat cheese made by non-Jews, or milk milked by a gentile unsupervised by a Jew, or bread of a gentile householder, or even bread of a Jew that was baked by a gentile without a Jew placing a stick in the oven [to mark participation]. And regarding food cooked by gentiles, even an egg roasted before us, even over a fire lit by a Jew and in a Jew's vessel [it is forbidden]. A pot in which a gentile cooked is forbidden to cook in without kashering it. Wine merely touched by a gentile, or any contact of a gentile with our wine, renders it forbidden. It is forbidden to eat with an evil, stingy eye, even if he is wealthy. It is forbidden to fix a [large] meal on the eve of Shabbat. But, excluding the deceased [may they rest], it is forbidden to eat the first mourner's meal [prepared by oneself]; and some say every first meal of the day is [not to be prepared for oneself]. It is forbidden to fix a meal during a public sermon on Shabbat, and certainly on a weekday, for everyone is obligated to go and listen, in order to learn, to observe, to perform and to fulfill.
Pele Yoetz 198:47: [20] Positive commandments from the Torah that depend on the hands and the whole body and can be fulfilled every day: The commandment of honoring father and mother also depends on action — feeding and giving drink, clothing and putting on shoes, bringing in and taking out, and serving them in every kind of service like a servant to his master. And he is obligated to set aside his own work in order to serve them. And if the father has no money, the son is obligated even to hire himself out, or to go door to door, in order to honor his father and mother in all the ways mentioned. It is a commandment to make tzitzit and to wrap oneself in it. It is a commandment to put on tefillin of the arm and of the head. It is a commandment to touch the tefillin every so often. It is a commandment to affix a mezuzah, and it is a commandment to place one's hand upon the mezuzah always when entering and leaving the house, and to remember that the blessed Name is the Master of the house and of everything in the house, and that He guards His people Israel. It is a commandment to make a parapet, a fence, and a covering wherever there is concern of mishap, and by considering this commandment every day and checking whether it needs repair, it is accounted to him as though he fulfills the commandment every day.
Pele Yoetz 198:48: It is a commandment to give charity with a good heart and joy, in accordance with the blessing the Lord has given him. It is a commandment to lend, whether as a loan of an object or of money, to poor and rich alike — “the world is built on kindness.” Repaying a debt is a commandment. It is a commandment to pay a hired worker's wages on time. It is a commandment to return a lost object. It is a commandment to return a pledge to a poor person at the time he needs it, and to take something else from him in its place. It is a commandment to return what was robbed, stolen, obtained through fraud, exploitation, interest, and the like. It is a commandment to perform acts of kindness, to visit the sick and to bury the dead. It is a commandment to go beyond the strict letter of the law. Some say it is a commandment to lend to a gentile with interest. It is a commandment to keep scales, weights, and measures honest. It is a commandment to save a fellow Israelite from any kind of danger by every possible means. It is a commandment to fulfill vows and what has come from one's lips — a statement to the Most High is like a vow. The commandment of separating the firstborn of an animal. The commandment of sending away the mother bird. It is a commandment to unload a burden from a fellow's animal, and certainly from the fellow himself (without needing the verse “when you see,” contrary to the custom of scoffers [who say the verse alone requires it]); and it is likewise a commandment to help load it back on. The commandment of covering the blood [of a slaughtered wild animal or fowl]. It is a commandment to serve a Torah scholar, and its reward is greater than that of studying under him (Berachot 7b). It is a commandment to redeem a firstborn from his mother. It is a commandment to take trouble over the lost item of our brethren until it is sought out for him, and certainly it is a commandment to take trouble for our brethren themselves, and “bring the poor who are cast out into your house.” It is a commandment to write a Torah scroll and to acquire other books. It is a commandment for a kohen to become impure for the seven relatives specified in the Torah, and included in this is the commandment of mourning for them. To whiten or kasher through hagalah vessels that were used by gentiles. It is a commandment for a person's hands to be folded one over the other on his heart, like a servant before his master, at the time of prayer. It is a commandment to save the pursued from the hand of the pursuer. To refrain from labor on Shabbat, Yom Kippur, Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot and Rosh Hashanah. It is a commandment to add from the mundane to the holy at its entrance and its departure. It is a commandment to make a sukkah and dwell in it. It is a commandment to take the lulav. It is a commandment to refrain from certain kinds of labor during the intermediate days of a festival. It is a commandment to nullify chametz on the eve of Passover before the sixth hour. It is a commandment to write laws, ethical teachings, introductions, commentaries and the like, and to print them to benefit the many immediately and for generations — there is no kindness greater than this, and “he who does kindness benefits his own soul.”
Pele Yoetz 198:49: [21] Negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the hands and can be kept every day: Not to worship idolatry. Not to make an idol. Not to make a raised human image even for ornamentation. Not to derive benefit from idolatry, its accessories, or its covering. “You shall not murder,” and one who publicly shames another is considered like a murderer. “You shall not steal.” “You shall not rob” — that is, taking by force, or anything against the owner's will without his complete willingness. “You shall not exploit” — this is when a fellow's money comes into his hand with the owner's consent, and he then refuses to pay; and even regarding a gentile, it is forbidden to steal from, rob, or exploit him. One who uses a pledge or a deposit belonging to his fellow is considered a thief, and even one who steals for his fellow's own benefit, to cause him distress so that he will be careful in guarding his belongings, is also considered a thief — even one who steals his own item back from the thief is a robber [of due process]. One who lends an item without the owner's permission is called a robber. It is forbidden to deceive people's minds, even a gentile's mind, through words. If one knows that his merchandise has a defect, he must inform the buyer. One should not touch up old vessels to make them appear new. One should not sell the meat of a carcass as though it were properly slaughtered meat. One should not select the grain visible on top of the storage bin to make the buyer think it is all equally sorted. One should not offer abundant hospitality to someone he knows will not accept it (though this may be permitted for the sake of peace). One should not press someone to eat when he knows he will not eat (though here too, it may depend on the person — for some, being urged is itself a mark of honor). And all similar cases are included in the prohibition of “you shall not wrong.”
Pele Yoetz 198:50: Not to be lazy in saving a fellow's property from damage, and not to turn a blind eye, and all the more so regarding saving our fellows themselves, and to offer counsel to help them in their time of trouble. Not to lend and not to borrow with interest, and not to be a guarantor, scribe, or witness for a loan with interest. That a hired worker's wages should not remain overnight [unpaid]. Not to ignore a situation when one sees a fellow's animal crouching under its burden, and all the more so if one sees his fellow himself crouching under a burden, for he transgresses a prohibition if he does not help him. Not to seize a debtor's pledge by force. Not to delay giving him back his pledge when he needs it. Not to take a pledge from a widow, and not to damage utensils used for preparing food, such as kneading and cooking vessels, or a slaughtering knife. Some say it is even forbidden to take these as a pledge at the time the loan is made; others say it is forbidden only when not at the time the loan is made. Not to bind a bride and groom to prevent their intimacy, and the wicked person who does this has no atonement ever and no share in the World to Come. Not to encroach on a boundary and expand one's territory, entering into a fellow's territory even by a finger's breadth. Not to erase the [divine] Name. Not to destroy a fruit tree, and included in this prohibition is that a person should be careful with his money and not waste even the value of a perutah in vain. Not to cook meat with milk even to feed it to a gentile or for any other purpose. If one saw or heard that a fellow Israelite is in danger, he is obligated to strive for his rescue with all his strength and might, and likewise if he was sick, he is obligated to strive for his healing, and one who is lazy about it is considered a shedder of blood, and of this it is said (Leviticus 19:16), “You shall not stand idly by your fellow's blood.” Not to accept a bribe, and even a bribe of mere words is forbidden (Ketubot 105b). And one must refrain from judging someone from whom he has received any benefit whatsoever near the time of judgment. Not to delay burying the dead, unless it is for his honor.
Pele Yoetz 198:51: Not to round off the corner of the head [side-locks]. Not to destroy the corner of the beard, and it is even forbidden to pass a razor beneath the beard. A man's article should not be on a woman, and a man should not wear a woman's garment (Deuteronomy 22:5). (And it is not a good custom in some places to place women's jewelry on the groom's head on his wedding night. After his sins have been forgiven, this would be the first item in the reckoning of sins.) And it is forbidden to pluck white hairs from among black ones or to dye them. Likewise it is forbidden to look in a mirror, even casually and playfully, for Scripture did not distinguish between a fixed and a casual act, and it is not permitted even for the joy of a bride and groom or the joy of Purim and the like, for in the place of a commandment it becomes a transgression. Regarding removing hair from the armpit and pubic area, some say it is forbidden by Torah law and others say it is forbidden by rabbinic law, and even where men [normally] remove it, it is forbidden for a Jew to remove it [in that manner].
Pele Yoetz 198:52: Not to strike a fellow Israelite, whether great or small, man or woman, even his own wife, and from the moment he raises his hand he is called wicked and disqualified from testifying; and it is only permitted to strike for the purpose of discipline and rebuke, such as a father striking his son or a teacher his student and the like. A person should not enslave his fellow, and if they are in awe of him or ashamed to disobey his word, he should not command them to do anything, small or great, except by their own will, for their own benefit. Not to slaughter a mother animal and its young on the same day. Not to perform labor with two different species of animal, and even without labor, if they are tied together, such as pulling a horse by its bridle while a donkey tied behind the horse by a rope like the horse's harness — this is forbidden. And some say even without tying them together, such as riding a horse while pulling a dog on a leash beside the horse, is forbidden due to [the prohibition of] mixed kinds. And to drive two different species of animal even by voice alone is forbidden. Therefore it is forbidden to greet a gentile who is driving mixed species, since sometimes the animals hasten to move on account of the voice [used in the greeting]. Not to mate an animal, beast, or fowl with a different species.
Pele Yoetz 198:53: Not to graft one kind of tree onto another kind of tree, even outside the Land of Israel, and it is even forbidden to tell a gentile to graft mixed species for a Jew. Not to withhold one's hand from giving charity according to one's proper measure. Not to add to the commandments and not to subtract from them. Not to follow the customs of idolaters in their dress, their practices, and the ways of the Emorites; rather, Israel should be set apart from them in everything. Not to gash oneself over the dead. Not to form separate factions, meaning there should not be two courts in one city, one following one custom and the other following a different custom. Not to refrain from making a parapet, and included in this is to distance every kind of harm — not to raise a vicious dog and not to set up a rickety ladder and the like. A kohen should not become impure for the dead and should not enter a house where there is a corpse. And some authorities rule that gentile graves render one impure just like graves of Israel (Tosafot, Bava Metzia 114b). And it is forbidden for a kohen to enter a cemetery even to his father's grave, for on his return he will render others impure. Not to wrong another in measure or weight, even a gentile, whether by selling less than the proper amount or buying more than the proper amount, and the punishment for [dishonest] measures is severe (Yevamot 21a). Indeed, it is even forbidden to keep in one's house measures that are short or excessive, even to use them as a chamber pot; rather, one is obligated to break any vessel made for [dishonest] measures. Not to castrate any species, neither man, nor beast, nor fowl, and it is even forbidden to tell a gentile to castrate an animal. Not to delay fulfilling vows; and a person who says he will give charity to the poor, even though he did not utter the word “vow” with his mouth, it is considered a full vow and he is obligated to give it immediately. And even if he delays due to forgetfulness, he will be punished in that his young children and his wife will die, God forbid. Not to transgress one's vow or oath except through formal annulment. A person should not commit a transgression or do a deed that desecrates the Name of Heaven through it. And a Torah scholar, or a person who maintains a reputation for uprightness, whose conduct is not meticulously careful and causes people to speak ill of him — this is a desecration of the Name. And those who lie to gentiles and steal from them are included among those who desecrate the Name, for they cause the gentiles to say that Israel has no Torah, and the sin of desecrating the Name is graver than the sins punishable by karet or death at the hands of a court. Not to perform labor on Shabbat and festivals. Chametz shall not be seen and shall not be found [on Passover].
Pele Yoetz 198:54: [22] Positive and negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the hands: The commandment of washing hands before eating or before eating something dipped in liquid. The commandment of Mayim Acharonim [washing after the meal] is obligatory (Eruvin 17b; Chullin 105b), and one who is lax about it shortens his days and years, and the holy Zohar (Devarim, p. 273) is very strict about it. The commandment of washing hands before prayer even if one's hands are [already] clean. The commandment of kindling the Shabbat candle. The commandment of kindling the Chanukah candle. The commandment of the eruv of courtyards. The commandment of the eruv tavshilin, [permitting] cooking on a festival for Shabbat. Since the destruction of the Temple, our sages, of blessed memory, instituted (Orach Chaim 560:2) that when a groom marries, he takes ashes from a burnt object and places them on his head at the spot where tefillin are placed. Likewise, when a house is plastered with lime, one square amah opposite the entrance is left without lime. Gifts to the poor that are biblically mandated in the Land of Israel, such as pe'ah, gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the poor man's tithe and the gleanings of a vineyard, are obligatory outside the Land by rabbinic decree. It is forbidden for a person to perform labor from when dawn breaks until he has prayed the morning prayer. It is forbidden to perform labor on the eves of Shabbat and festivals from the time of Minchah onward, and on the eve of Passover from midday it is forbidden. A mourner is forbidden to put on tefillin on the first day, and on the second day until sunrise, and for all three days he is forbidden to perform labor, even a poor person who is supported by charity. From this point onward [after three days], a poor person may work privately within his home. Since the destruction of the Temple, our sages, of blessed memory, decreed (Gittin 7a) not to play musical instruments, and it is forbidden to use any sound-producing device for rejoicing, and it is forbidden to listen to them; even singing with the mouth is forbidden unless it is a song and praise of the Holy One, blessed be He. It is forbidden by rabbinic law to sow mixed seeds of the vineyard outside the Land of Israel.
